Park Landscape at the Hunting Château Moritzburg - Ernst Ferdinand Oehme

The motif of the view from the foot of the stairs of Moritzburg Castle across the large pond repeatedly occupied Ernst Ferdinand Oehme between 1844 and 1853. Individual nature studies of the balustrade, the sculpture of a horn player and the lake (Neidhardt WV 207, 208, 209) prepared the now lost painting, which under the title "The Triumph of Nature" caused such a sensation at the exhibition of the Saxon Art Association in 1845, that it was discussed by the Dresden art pope Johann Gottlob von Quandt in a lengthy article in the Dresdner Abendzeitung. It can be assumed that a watercolor with the same title from 1847 (Neidhardt WV 240) is largely identical to the lost picture, which the artist repeated in a slightly different version in 1849 (Neidhardt WV 251). In 1853, Oehme created another watercolor replica of the apparently very popular motif (Neidhardt WV 271). The present, undated version in oil paints differs from all other known variants of the motif in one important detail: the right of the two horn players overhangs the tree backdrop with half its body and stands out sharply against the reddish-yellow sky. Ernst Ferdinand Oehme uses the vanitas theme, which has been known in art history since antiquity and the Christian Middle Ages, on which German Romanticism has expressed itself in its own varied way. But it is not the Gothic church ruins of Caspar David Friedrich, but stone relics of the courtly baroque that become symbols of transience for him. The strongest symbol for this is probably that overturned rococo vase on the lake shore, overgrown by plants. Quandt speaks of “natural forces that work to dissolve that stone that has been deformed by human hands”, and thus expresses the rejection of the Baroque style prevailing at the time. Compared to the aforementioned watercolor versions, Oehme's painting skills are evident in the color implementation of the evening mood and the desertedness of the place.
